title: Integer factoring: classical algorithms vs Shor's quantum algorithm
problem_statement: Given a composite integer N, output a nontrivial factor of N.

algorithms.name: trial division
algorithms.pseudocode: for d = 2, 3, ...: if d | N return d

algorithms.name: Pollard rho
algorithms.idea: Iterate a pseudo-random map x -> x^2 + c mod N and detect a collision modulo an unknown prime factor via gcd.
algorithms.time_complexity: O(N^(1/4)) = O(2^(n/4)) heuristically (birthday bound on the smallest prime factor)

algorithms.name: general number field sieve (GNFS)
algorithms.idea: Find many smooth relations in two number rings, combine them by linear algebra over GF(2) into a congruence of squares.
algorithms.time_complexity: exp(((64/9)^(1/3) + o(1)) (ln N)^(1/3) (ln ln N)^(2/3)), i.e. L_N[1/3, 1.923]: sub-exponential (heuristic)
algorithms.correctness: Heuristic running time; output is checkable (a factor is verified by one division).

algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm
algorithms.idea: Reduce factoring to order finding; find the order of a random a mod N with the quantum Fourier transform.
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n^3) quantum gates with schoolbook modular arithmetic (O(n^2 log n log log n) with fast multiplication)
algorithms.correctness: Shor 1997 (succeeds with constant probability per run).

relationship: No classical polynomial-time algorithm is known; the best classical algorithms are sub-exponential (heuristically L[1/3]; rigorously L[1/2] randomized, Lenstra-Pomerance 1992). Shor's algorithm is polynomial on a quantum computer.

sources.title: A Monte Carlo method for factorization

sources.title: The development of the number field sieve

sources.title: Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer

caveats: Factoring is NOT known to be NP-hard and is in NP intersect coNP, so it is not believed to be NP-complete. Catalogued as OPEN (T6). This project does not target factoring operationally (START_HERE section 10).
notes: Central evidence for quantum advantage: a problem believed hard classically with a polynomial quantum algorithm. No theorem we know of rules out a classical polynomial algorithm; one would only break the belief that factoring is hard (and much deployed cryptography).
